trap.title: Exclusion, not uncertainty
trap.body: Two famous quantum “principles” get mixed up all the time. This one is about crowding: no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers. Heisenberg’s uncertainty principle is about measuring: you cannot know a particle’s exact position and exact momentum at the same time. Hund’s rule and the Aufbau principle are separate electron-filling rules that also have their own answer lines.
trap.fix: Opposite spins, two electrons per orbital, quantum numbers, fermions, or white dwarfs mean this principle. Position, momentum, h-bar, or Heisenberg means the uncertainty principle, and electrons spreading out into empty orbitals before pairing up means Hund’s rule.
trap.line: Real answer line: Pauli exclusion principle (accept exclusion principle or Pauli principle; prompt on Pauli; do not accept “uncertainty principle”)

topics.name: Michael Faraday
topics.kicker: Self-taught English experimenter · Discovered electromagnetic induction
topics.briefing: Michael Faraday was a blacksmith’s son with little schooling who taught himself science as a bookbinder’s apprentice, reading the books he bound. After Humphry Davy hired him at London’s Royal Institution, Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831, the idea behind electric generators. He also built an early electric motor, discovered benzene, and started the Royal Institution’s Christmas Lectures for young people.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1845, this scientist found that a magnet can rotate the direction in which light vibrates inside heavy glass, the first evidence that light and magnetism are linked. That year, he also showed that materials like bismuth are weakly pushed away by magnets, an effect he called diamagnetism.
tossups.r: He is best known for discovering electromagnetic induction in 1831. For 10 points, name this English scientist.

tossups.p: In 1825, this scientist isolated a new compound from the oily leftovers of the gas used for lighting, calling it “bicarburet of hydrogen.” That compound was later named benzene. Two years earlier, he had squeezed chlorine gas into a liquid.
tossups.r: His 1831 experiments showed that a moving magnet can create an electric current in a coil of wire. For 10 points, name this English scientist.

tossups.p: In 1821, soon after Hans Christian Ørsted found that electric currents make compass needles turn, this scientist made a hanging wire carrying a current spin around a magnet standing in a bowl of mercury. That device was an early electric motor.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English scientist who later discovered electromagnetic induction and built an early generator.

tossups.p: In August 1831, this scientist wrapped two coils of wire around opposite sides of an iron ring and saw a galvanometer’s needle jump only when the current in one coil was switched on or off. Joseph Henry found the same effect on his own in the United States.
tossups.r: That effect is called electromagnetic induction. For 10 points, name this English scientist who also built an early electric motor.

tossups.p: This scientist made an early generator out of a copper disk that spun between the poles of a horseshoe magnet, producing a steady current. His law of induction says a changing magnetic field through a loop of wire creates a voltage in the loop.
tossups.r: Transformers and the generators in power plants rely on that law. For 10 points, name this English scientist.

tossups.p: With help from the scholar William Whewell [“HYOO-el”], this scientist introduced the words anode, cathode, and ion. The first of his two laws of electrolysis says that the amount of a substance made at an electrode is proportional to the electric charge that flows.
tossups.r: A constant of about 96,485 coulombs per mole is named for him. For 10 points, name this English scientist.

tossups.p: This scientist’s holiday talks about candles were published as _The Chemical History of a Candle_, which explains that a burning candle makes water and carbon dioxide. In 1825, he started the Royal Institution’s yearly Christmas Lectures for young people.
tossups.r: He also built an early electric motor. For 10 points, name this English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: As a teenage apprentice to a London bookbinder, this future scientist taught himself by reading the books he bound, including Jane Marcet’s _Conversations on Chemistry_. He later bound his own notes from Humphry Davy’s lectures into a book and sent it to Davy, hoping for a job.
tossups.r: Davy hired him as an assistant in 1813. For 10 points, name this English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: James Clerk Maxwell built on this scientist’s idea of invisible “lines of force” stretching around magnets and electric charges, writing a paper named for those lines. This scientist sprinkled iron filings around magnets to make the lines visible.
tossups.r: The SI unit of capacitance is named for him. For 10 points, name this English discoverer of electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: In 1857, this scientist made a ruby-red liquid that held specks of gold far too small to see, and he concluded that its color came from gold broken into extremely tiny particles. Earlier, he had discovered benzene and turned chlorine gas into a liquid.
tossups.r: He spent his career at London’s Royal Institution. For 10 points, name this English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: To show that electric charge stays on the outside of a conductor, this scientist built a room covered in metal foil and showed that sparks striking the outside left the inside uncharged. The metal mesh in a microwave oven’s door works the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this English scientist, whose name is on cages that block outside electric fields.

tossups.p: This scientist, a member of a small Christian group called the Sandemanians, turned down a knighthood. Queen Victoria gave him a house at Hampton Court, where he died in 1867. He was the son of a blacksmith and had little formal schooling.
tossups.r: He built an early electric motor in 1821. For 10 points, name this English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: From 1813 to 1815, this young man traveled across Europe as the assistant of the chemist who first isolated sodium and potassium. It is often said that this man was the greatest discovery of that chemist, Humphry Davy.
tossups.r: He also discovered benzene. For 10 points, name this English scientist who discovered electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: Albert Einstein kept a picture of this scientist on the wall of his study, along with one of James Clerk Maxwell. This scientist’s law of induction explains how transformers raise or lower the voltage of electric power.
tossups.r: A constant equal to the charge on one mole of electrons is named for him. For 10 points, name this English scientist, the discoverer of electromagnetic induction.

tossups.p: In an 1855 letter to _The Times_, this scientist described dropping white cards into the River Thames from a boat to show how murky the water had become. This scientist also made an early generator from a copper disk spinning near a magnet.
tossups.r: His law of induction explains how generators work. For 10 points, name this English scientist.

Built an early electric motor (1821) and an early electric generator
The SI unit of capacitance is named for him
Metal cages named for him block outside electric fields; the mesh in a microwave oven’s door works the same way
His law of induction: a changing magnetic field through a loop of wire creates a voltage; transformers and generators rely on it

A blacksmith’s son with little schooling, he taught himself science as a bookbinder’s apprentice
Discovered benzene in 1825, calling it “bicarburet of hydrogen”
In his iron ring experiment (1831), switching the current in one coil on or off briefly made a current in a second coil
Made an early generator from a copper disk spinning between the poles of a horseshoe magnet
A constant of about 96,485 coulombs per mole, the charge on one mole of electrons, is named for him
Stated two laws of electrolysis; with William Whewell’s help, introduced the words anode, cathode, and ion
Pictured invisible “lines of force” around magnets, shown with iron filings; James Clerk Maxwell later turned his ideas into equations
Started the Royal Institution’s Christmas Lectures (1825); his talks became _The Chemical History of a Candle_
In 1845, showed that a magnet can rotate the direction light vibrates in heavy glass, the first evidence linking light and magnetism
Showed that materials like bismuth are weakly pushed away by magnets, an effect he called diamagnetism
In 1823, squeezed chlorine gas into a liquid
His 1821 motor, built soon after Ørsted’s discovery, made a current-carrying wire spin around a magnet in a bowl of mercury
The American Joseph Henry discovered induction independently at about the same time
Read Jane Marcet’s _Conversations on Chemistry_ while binding books
Traveled across Europe as Davy’s assistant from 1813 to 1815; often called Davy’s greatest discovery
In 1857, made a ruby-red liquid holding specks of gold far too small to see
Built a room covered in metal foil to show that sparks striking the outside left the inside uncharged
A member of a small Christian group called the Sandemanians; turned down a knighthood
Queen Victoria gave him a house at Hampton Court, where he died in 1867
Albert Einstein kept his picture on his study wall, along with a picture of James Clerk Maxwell

trap.title: Not Davy or Maxwell
trap.body: Several scientists tangle together in tossups about electricity and magnetism. Humphry Davy was this man’s boss and mentor, famous for isolating sodium and potassium with electricity. James Clerk Maxwell later turned this man’s “lines of force” into equations, and the American Joseph Henry discovered induction on his own at about the same time. Separate tossups also ask for the law, the cage, or the constant named for this man.
trap.fix: Bookbinding, benzene, the iron ring, the copper disk, the candle lectures, or the Royal Institution mean this man. Sodium, potassium, and the miner’s safety lamp mean Davy; a set of four famous equations means Maxwell; and if a question asks for “this law” or “this effect,” name the law or effect instead of the man.

topics.name: Reflection
topics.kicker: Waves bouncing off a surface · How mirrors and echoes work
topics.dates: Law known since ancient Greek times
topics.briefing: Reflection is what happens when a wave bounces off a surface instead of passing through it. A smooth mirror sends light away at the same angle it arrived, which keeps the image sharp, and sound bouncing off a canyon wall comes back as an echo. Even moonlight is just sunlight bouncing off the Moon’s surface.
topics.answerHtml: reflection (accept word forms like reflecting; accept specific types such as specular reflection, diffuse reflection, or total internal reflection; do not accept “refraction” or “diffraction”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Apollo astronauts left panels of corner-cube prisms on the Moon that send laser light straight back toward Earth, letting scientists measure that the Moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year. Bicycle and road-sign safety markers work the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of a wave off a surface, which lets you see yourself in a mirror.

tossups.p: Hero of Alexandria showed that light traveling from an object to a flat, polished surface and then to an eye takes the shortest possible route, an early version of Fermat’s principle. The incoming ray, the outgoing ray, and the line perpendicular to the surface, called the normal, all lie in one plane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect described by a law stating that light leaves a mirror at the same angle at which it arrived.

tossups.p: At Brewster’s angle, light bouncing off a sheet of glass becomes completely polarized, and the bounced ray and the bent ray travel at right angles to each other. Polarized sunglasses cut glare because light bouncing off a flat road or lake is partly polarized.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which makes the image you see in a mirror.

tossups.p: The Fresnel [“fray-NEL”] equations give the fraction of light sent back at a boundary between two materials; for light hitting ordinary glass straight on, that fraction is only about 4 percent. That is why you can faintly see yourself in a shop window.
tossups.r: A flat mirror uses this effect to make an upright image that seems to sit behind the glass. For 10 points, name this bouncing of a wave off a surface.

tossups.p: Coatings on eyeglasses and camera lenses are made about a quarter of a wavelength thick, so the light waves bouncing back from the top and bottom of each coating cancel out and glare is reduced. Stealth aircraft are shaped to send radar waves away from the receiver instead of back toward it.
tossups.r: Smooth surfaces make a sharp “specular” kind of this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light, which lets a mirror form an image.

tossups.p: A pulse sent along a rope tied to a wall comes back upside down, while a pulse on a rope with a loose end comes back right side up. Light picks up a similar half-wavelength flip when it bounces off a material in which it travels more slowly.
tossups.r: Echoes are an example of this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of waves off a surface.

tossups.p: Past the critical angle, light inside glass cannot escape through the surface and all of it bounces back inside, which lets optical fibers carry signals over long distances. The same trick makes a cut diamond sparkle and lets prisms fold the light path inside binoculars.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which is how a mirror works.

tossups.p: A layer behind the retina called the tapetum lucidum [“tuh-PEE-tum LOO-sih-dum”] makes the eyes of cats and deer glow in headlights by sending light back through the eye. Road markers called “cat’s eyes” use glass beads or prisms to send headlight beams back toward drivers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a wave bounces off a surface, as light does from a mirror.

tossups.p: In 1668, Isaac Newton built a telescope that gathered light with a curved metal dish instead of a glass lens, which avoided the colored fringes that lenses create. Most large modern telescopes also collect light with curved surfaces instead of lenses, and the James Webb Space Telescope’s curved surfaces are coated with gold.
tossups.r: Those telescopes depend on this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which lets a mirror form an image.

tossups.p: David Brewster patented the kaleidoscope in 1817; its endlessly repeating patterns come from light bouncing back and forth between two or three long, shiny strips set at an angle. Submarine crews use periscopes, which bounce light off two surfaces tilted at 45 degrees, to look above the water.
tossups.r: Both devices rely on mirrors. For 10 points, name this effect in which light bounces off a surface.

tossups.p: A surface’s albedo is the fraction of sunlight it sends back; fresh snow has a very high albedo, and dark ocean water has a low one. Saturn’s icy moon Enceladus [“en-SEL-uh-dus”] sends back most of the sunlight that hits it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface, which lets you see yourself in a mirror.

tossups.p: Leonardo da Vinci correctly explained the faint glow on the dark part of a crescent Moon, called earthshine, as sunlight bounced off Earth and then off the Moon. Ordinary moonlight is also just sunlight sent back by the Moon’s surface.
tossups.r: Because of this effect, drivers can read the backward word “AMBULANCE” on an ambulance’s front in their rearview mirrors. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface.

tossups.p: Legends claim that Archimedes used polished bronze shields to focus sunlight and set Roman ships on fire during the siege of Syracuse. Solar power towers use fields of shiny panels to aim sunlight at one spot in the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which light bounces off a shiny surface, such as a mirror.

tossups.p: A car headlight puts its bulb at the focus of a curved, bowl-shaped surface, so the light leaves in a parallel beam; a satellite dish works the same way in reverse. For a spherical curve, that focus lies halfway between the surface and its center of curvature.
tossups.r: Concave and convex mirrors both rely on this effect. For 10 points, name this bouncing of light off a surface.

tossups.p: In the Whispering Gallery of St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, a whisper near the curved wall can be heard far across the dome because the sound keeps bouncing along the wall. Bats and dolphins find food by listening for sounds that come back to them.
tossups.r: Those returning sounds are echoes. For 10 points, name this bouncing of a wave off a surface.

trap.title: Bounce, bend, or spread?
trap.body: Reflection, refraction, and diffraction sound alike and all describe a wave meeting something, so real tossups are strict about which one they want. Reflection is a wave bouncing back off a surface and staying in the same material. Refraction is bending as the wave crosses into a new material and changes speed, and diffraction is spreading around an edge or through a narrow opening.
trap.fix: Mirrors, echoes, equal angles, albedo, or light sent back the way it came mean reflection. A bent straw, lenses, Snell’s law, or a prism means refraction; slits, gratings, Bragg’s law, or sound bending around corners means diffraction.
trap.line: Real answer line: reflection (accept word forms like reflecting; accept specific types such as specular reflection, diffuse reflection, or total internal reflection; do not accept “refraction” or “diffraction”)

topics.name: Diffraction
topics.kicker: Waves spreading around edges · Why you can hear around corners
topics.dates: Named by Grimaldi in a book published in 1665
topics.briefing: Diffraction is the spreading of a wave as it squeezes through a gap or bends around the edge of an obstacle. It is why you can hear a friend talking around a corner even when you cannot see them: sound waves are long enough to bend around the wall, but light waves are much too short. Shining light through tiny slits makes striped patterns that helped prove light is a wave.
topics.answerHtml: diffraction (accept word forms like diffracting; accept specific types such as X-ray diffraction, electron diffraction, or single-slit diffraction; do not accept “refraction” or “interference”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When Augustin-Jean Fresnel [“fray-NEL”] entered a contest on this effect in 1818, Siméon Denis Poisson [“pwah-SOHN”] argued that Fresnel’s wave theory predicted an absurd result: a bright spot in the center of a round object’s shadow. François Arago [“ah-rah-GOH”] then found that spot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this spreading of a wave as it passes the edge of an obstacle or goes through a narrow opening.

tossups.p: The Jesuit priest Francesco Maria Grimaldi named this effect after the Latin for “breaking into pieces,” in a book published in 1665, after he saw that light passing a thin rod made a shadow edged with colored bands.
tossups.r: Waves spread out the most when an opening is about as wide as their wavelength. For 10 points, name this bending of waves around obstacles.

tossups.p: A principle named for Jacques Babinet [“bah-bee-NAY”] says that a thin hair and a slit of the same width produce nearly the same pattern from this effect, so a laser shining past a hair can measure its thickness. Narrowing a slit makes the pattern of light and dark bands spread out wider.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which waves spread out after passing through a narrow opening or around an edge.

tossups.p: Light passing through a round opening makes a bright central spot called an Airy disk, surrounded by faint rings. According to the Rayleigh criterion, two stars can just be told apart when the center of one’s spot falls on the first dark ring of the other’s.
tossups.r: This effect sets a limit on how sharp a telescope’s images can be. For 10 points, name this spreading of waves around edges and through openings.

tossups.p: William Lawrence Bragg was 25 when he and his father shared the 1915 Nobel Prize in Physics; his law, n lambda equals 2 d sine theta, uses this effect to find the spacing between layers of atoms in a crystal.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, used in X-ray crystallography, in which waves spread out as they pass edges or narrow gaps.

tossups.p: In 1912, Max von Laue [“LOW-uh”] showed that a crystal could act on X-rays the way a fine grid of slits acts on light, proving that X-rays are waves and that crystals are made of regularly spaced atoms. The resulting patterns of spots let scientists work out where atoms sit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this spreading of waves as they pass through narrow openings or around edges.

tossups.p: In 1927, Clinton Davisson and Lester Germer fired electrons at a nickel crystal and saw the kind of pattern only waves make, confirming an idea of Louis de Broglie [“duh BROY”] that particles act like waves. George Paget Thomson saw the same effect with electrons passing through thin metal foil.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which waves spread out after passing through a narrow opening or around an edge.

tossups.p: Rosalind Franklin’s “Photo 51,” made by sending X-rays through fibers of DNA, showed an X-shaped pattern from this effect that revealed the molecule’s helical shape. X-rays work for this because their wavelengths are about as small as the spaces between atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, the spreading of waves around obstacles and through small gaps.

tossups.p: Ernst Abbe [“AH-buh”] showed that this effect keeps ordinary light microscopes from seeing details much smaller than about half the wavelength of light. Eric Betzig, Stefan Hell, and William Moerner shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for microscopes that get around that limit.
tossups.r: Electron microscopes suffer less from it because electrons have much shorter wavelengths. For 10 points, name this spreading of waves around obstacles.

tossups.p: A small, colorful ring called a corona that sometimes surrounds the Moon is caused by this effect in tiny water droplets, unlike the much larger 22-degree halo, which comes from light bending through ice crystals. Iridescent clouds get their colors in a similar way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this spreading of light waves around small obstacles and through narrow gaps.

tossups.p: David Rittenhouse made an early grating for this effect in 1785 by stretching hairs between two fine screws. The rainbow colors on the back of a CD appear because its tightly packed rows of pits act as a grating, sending each color off at a different angle.
tossups.r: Spectroscopes use gratings that rely on this effect. For 10 points, name this spreading of waves through narrow slits.

tossups.p: AM radio signals, whose waves are hundreds of meters long, curve around hills and tall buildings much better than FM signals because of this effect. Ocean waves fan out in the same way after passing through a narrow harbor entrance.
tossups.r: This effect lets you hear someone talking around a corner. For 10 points, name this spreading of waves around obstacles.

tossups.p: The spikes seen around bright stars in many telescope photos come from this effect, as starlight passes the thin struts that hold a telescope’s second mirror. The bigger a telescope’s opening, the less this effect blurs its images.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this spreading of light as it passes the edge of an object or goes through a narrow slit.

tossups.p: The Huygens–Fresnel [“HOY-gunz fray-NEL”] principle explains this effect by treating every point on a wave’s front as the source of tiny new wavelets that spread out and overlap. Far from an opening, the simpler Fraunhofer [“FROWN-hoh-fer”] form of this effect applies.
tossups.r: In a single-slit pattern, the central bright band is twice as wide as the others. For 10 points, name this spreading of waves through openings.

tossups.p: In the early 1800s, Thomas Young sent light through two narrow slits and saw stripes of light and dark, evidence that light is a wave. Each slit spreads the light out because of this effect, and the overlapping waves then interfere.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this bending of waves around obstacles, which is different from refraction and interference.

trap.title: Not refraction or interference
trap.body: Diffraction, refraction, and interference all show up in optics tossups, and real answer lines keep them apart. Refraction is bending when a wave crosses into a new material and changes speed. Interference is what happens when overlapping waves add up or cancel out, and in a two-slit experiment both effects happen at once: each slit spreads the light by diffraction, and the spreading waves then interfere.
trap.fix: Edges, narrow gaps, gratings, X-ray crystals, Bragg’s law, Airy disks, or sound bending around corners mean diffraction. A straw that looks bent, lenses, or Snell’s law mean refraction; if a question stresses two waves adding up or canceling, as in soap bubbles or noise-canceling headphones, the answer may be interference.
trap.line: Real answer line: diffraction (accept word forms like diffracting; accept specific types such as X-ray diffraction, electron diffraction, or single-slit diffraction; do not accept “refraction” or “interference”)

topics.name: Protons
topics.kicker: Positive particles in every nucleus · Their count sets the element
topics.briefing: Protons are the positively charged particles packed into the nucleus of every atom, and the number of them decides which element an atom is: one for hydrogen, six for carbon, 79 for gold. Each proton is about 1,836 times heavier than an electron and is built from three smaller particles called quarks. Ernest Rutherford named the particle in 1920, from the Greek word for “first.”
topics.answerHtml: protons (accept hydrogen nuclei or hydrogen ions; prompt on nucleons, baryons, or hadrons; do not accept “neutrons”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: A “radius puzzle” about this particle began in 2010, when experiments using hydrogen atoms with a muon in place of the electron found this particle smaller than expected. This particle is made of two up quarks and one down quark.
tossups.r: The strong force holds these particles together in nuclei despite their electric repulsion. For 10 points, name this positively charged particle found in the nucleus of every atom.

tossups.p: Only about one percent of this particle’s mass comes from the masses of its quarks. This particle has a mass of about one atomic mass unit, and its charge, about 1.6 times ten to the negative nineteenth coulombs, is the same size as an electron’s.
tossups.r: Gluons hold its three quarks together. For 10 points, name this positive particle found in atomic nuclei along with neutrons.

tossups.p: In the late 1960s, electrons fired at this particle at the Stanford Linear Accelerator bounced off as if it held tiny, hard bits inside, which Richard Feynman called “partons.” Jerome Friedman, Henry Kendall, and Richard Taylor shared the 1990 Nobel Prize for those experiments.
tossups.r: Those bits turned out to be quarks. For 10 points, name this positively charged particle in the atomic nucleus.

tossups.p: In 1955, Emilio Segrè and Owen Chamberlain used the Bevatron at Berkeley to create the negatively charged antiparticle of this particle, winning the 1959 Nobel Prize in Physics. This particle is about 1,836 times as heavy as an electron.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this positively charged particle whose number in an atom’s nucleus gives the atomic number.

tossups.p: Some grand unified theories predict that this particle decays, but underground water tanks like Japan’s Super-Kamiokande have never seen it happen, showing that its lifetime is far longer than the age of the universe. A free neutron decays within minutes, but a free one of these particles is stable.
tossups.r: The simplest atom, hydrogen, has just one of these particles in its nucleus. For 10 points, name these positively charged nuclear particles.

tossups.p: Around 1917, Ernest Rutherford fired alpha particles into nitrogen gas and detected these particles being knocked out, often called the first artificial change of one element into another. In 1920 he named these particles after the Greek word for “first.”
tossups.r: Each one carries a charge equal and opposite to an electron’s. For 10 points, name these positive particles in every atomic nucleus.

tossups.p: In 1886, Eugen Goldstein found “canal rays” streaming backward through holes in the negative electrode of a gas-filled tube; in hydrogen gas, the lightest of those rays turned out to be these particles. Wilhelm Wien [“VEEN”] measured their charge-to-mass ratio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these positively charged particles that join neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

tossups.p: Cancer treatments using beams of this particle can target tumors deep in the body because the particles release most of their energy at one depth, called the Bragg peak, and then stop. MRI machines make pictures by tracking the magnetic spins of these particles in the body’s hydrogen atoms.
tossups.r: Henry Moseley showed that the periodic table should be ordered by the number of these particles in each atom. For 10 points, name these positive nuclear particles.

tossups.p: In water, a lone one of these particles never stays free for long; it quickly attaches to a water molecule to form the hydronium ion. Johannes Brønsted and Thomas Lowry defined acids as substances that give away these particles.
tossups.r: Bases accept them. For 10 points, name these positively charged particles found in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: The Large Hadron Collider near Geneva smashes together beams of these particles in a ring about 27 kilometers around, and its collisions led to the 2012 discovery of the Higgs boson. These particles are baryons, made of three quarks each.
tossups.r: Each has a charge of plus one. For 10 points, name these particles that, together with neutrons, make up atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: About nine out of ten cosmic-ray particles striking Earth’s atmosphere from space are these particles, which also make up much of the solar wind. In the Sun’s core, energy production begins when two of these particles fuse.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these positive particles whose number in a nucleus is an element’s atomic number.

tossups.p: In positron emission, one of these particles inside a nucleus changes into a neutron, giving off a positron and a neutrino. In electron capture, one of these particles absorbs an inner electron and also becomes a neutron.
tossups.r: In beta-minus decay, a neutron turns into one of these. For 10 points, name these positive particles in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: In 1932, John Cockcroft and Ernest Walton used a high-voltage machine to fire these particles at lithium, splitting lithium nuclei into pairs of alpha particles. That same year, James Chadwick discovered the neutral particle that shares the nucleus with these particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these positively charged nuclear particles, made of two up quarks and a down quark.

tossups.p: Peter Mitchell won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for showing that cells make ATP by letting these particles flow back across a membrane through the enzyme ATP synthase. In photosynthesis, these particles pile up inside thylakoids before rushing out through that enzyme.
tossups.r: Acids give them away. For 10 points, name these positive particles found in every atomic nucleus.

tossups.p: This particle is slightly lighter than the neutron. An atom’s mass number is found by adding the number of these particles to the number of neutrons, and in a neutral atom, the number of these particles equals the number of electrons.
tossups.r: Isotopes of an element all have the same number of these particles but different numbers of neutrons. For 10 points, name these positive nuclear particles.

trap.title: Which nuclear particle?
trap.body: Tossups about the atom have several look-alike answers. Neutrons sit in the nucleus too but have no charge, electrons orbit outside it with a negative charge, and quarks are the smaller pieces that make up both protons and neutrons. A clue about atomic number, positive charge, or acids giving something away points to this particle, while a neutral particle that James Chadwick found in 1932 is the neutron.
trap.fix: Positive charge, atomic number, the simplest nucleus, or two up quarks and a down quark mean this particle. No charge, Chadwick, or chain reactions mean the neutron; negative charge, J. J. Thomson, or orbitals mean the electron; and saying “nucleon” or “baryon” only earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: protons (accept hydrogen nuclei or hydrogen ions; prompt on nucleons, baryons, or hadrons; do not accept “neutrons”)
